title: Aguilar Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Aguilar wells have a 240 ft median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $14,400-$25,200.
h1: What Aguilar, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Aguilar means looking past the house and checking the well record. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records list 285 permitted wells. Depth, production and water level vary substantially across this plains setting, where permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers rather than Denver Basin aquifers.

The records provide useful local expectations, but they are not a guarantee for one lot. Only 192 wells report total depth, 62 report pump yield and 22 report static water level. Nearby wells around Lynn, El Moro and Hoehne can help establish a starting point for bids and due diligence.

sections.heading: Aguilar well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Aguilar is 240 feet. The middle half runs from 64 to 523 feet, so a driller’s bid based only on the median can miss the actual conditions by a wide margin. The 90th percentile is 780 feet, and the deepest record reaches 2,458 feet.

Depth is spread across the area: 31% of wells are under 100 feet, 24% are 100-300 feet, 23% are 300-600 feet and 21% are 600 feet or deeper. That mix reflects alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, along with fractured-bedrock conditions identified on the permits. Ask for a written bid that explains what happens if the hole must go deeper, and confirm casing and grout details before work starts.

sections.heading: Most Aguilar wells make usable water, but production still varies
sections.html:
Among the 62 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 4.0-9.0 gallons per minute. That is a reasonable planning range for a household, but the yield test does not replace storage and pressure-system design.

The local spread matters more than the median. Two percent of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, 34% produce 1-5 gallons per minute, 56% produce 5-15 gallons per minute and 8% produce more than 15 gallons per minute. A low-yield well may still work with a storage tank and careful demand management. Have the driller explain the test duration, recovery and proposed pump before you treat a yield number as dependable supply.

sections.heading: Aguilar water levels are shallow in some wells and deep in others
sections.html:
Only 22 permits in the local records report a static water level. Their median depth to water is 60 feet, with the middle half from 36 to 261 feet. This is a broad range, not a site-specific promise. A nearby water level can differ because of elevation, formation, season and pumping.

The permit counts by decade do not establish a water-table trend. They show 2 permits from the 1960s, 14 from the 1970s, 6 from the 1980s, 60 from the 1990s, 92 from the 2000s, 35 from the 2010s and 23 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, but the dataset does not provide enough decade-by-decade water-level information to conclude that groundwater is dropping or stable. Request a current measurement during inspection.

sections.heading: Permit activity and the drillers seen around Aguilar
sections.html:
Aguilar’s permit history is concentrated in more recent decades, with the largest recorded group from the 2000s. The records include domestic or household use on 66% of wells, stock use on 38%, irrigation on 5% and monitoring on 9%. A permit’s use designation matters when you plan a home, livestock operation or irrigation system.

The most active drillers in these records are Boday Well Drilling, associated with Kathleen Boday, with 38 wells; Weber Water Well Drilling & Pump Service LLC, associated with David J. Weber, with 24; and Boday Well Drilling, associated with Alex Boday, with 17. These are record counts, not endorsements. Check the construction report, permit status and final well test for the specific property.

sections.heading: What a new Aguilar well may cost
sections.html:
For Aguilar’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35-$55 per foot. At the local median depth of 240 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $8,400-$13,200.

A finished system is more than the hole. Including a pump, tank, trenching and electrical, the modeled total is about $14,400-$25,200 at that median depth. A lot requiring a deeper hole can exceed that range, while a shallow hole may cost less. Get the bid separated into drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, pressure tank, trenching, electrical and testing. Also ask which items are allowances and what charges apply if the hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: Aguilar lot risks include mines, PFAS and low-yield wells
sections.html:
Environmental due diligence deserves attention near Aguilar. Mapped records within about 10 miles include 36 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 187 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped set. These figures do not prove a problem on a particular parcel, but they are good reasons to check the property history, nearby land uses and available water-quality records.

Test the well for the contaminants relevant to the site and have the septic layout evaluated before closing. Keep the well, septic system and building location coordinated with access for drilling and maintenance. A fractured-bedrock or low-yield result can affect storage, pump selection and daily water use. If a proposed building site is remote or steep, price the access driveway, trenching and site work with the well rather than treating them as separate surprises.

sections.heading: A practical buying plan for land around Aguilar
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel and pull the DWR permit and construction record. Compare completed wells near Aguilar, Lynn and the other nearby areas in the data, but give the most weight to wells with similar elevation, geology and intended use. Confirm that the permit supports the home or other planned use; an exempt household-use well is not a substitute for checking current rules and site conditions.

Before closing, make the contract contingent on well inspection, water-quality testing and a septic feasibility review. Ask a licensed driller for a site-specific depth and cost range, including a dry-hole or low-yield plan. Colorado’s exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gallons per minute, but that legal limit is not a prediction of what the well will produce. Plan storage and conservation around the tested yield, not the best number in the neighborhood.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Aguilar, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Aguilar is 240 feet. The middle half runs from 64 to 523 feet, while the 90th percentile is 780 feet. Records range from shallow wells under 100 feet to a deepest reported depth of 2,458 feet, so local well depth can vary sharply from one parcel to another.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Aguilar?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 240-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,400-$13,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $14,400-$25,200. A deeper-than-median hole, difficult access or site-specific construction requirements can raise the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Aguilar wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 6.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 4.0-9.0 gallons per minute. Reported production varies: 34% of wells are in the 1-5 gallon-per-minute range and 56% are in the 5-15 range. Only 62 local records report yield, so test the specific well before relying on the number.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Aguilar?
faq.a: Well safety cannot be determined from a permit or a nearby yield record. The area has 36 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 187 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well for appropriate contaminants, review nearby land uses and retest after work on the well or septic system.

faq.q: Are Aguilar wells getting deeper or running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a local dropping water-table trend. Only 22 wells report static water level; their median depth to water is 60 feet and the middle half is 36-261 feet. Permit activity spans the 1960s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year 2025, but that does not substitute for a current measurement and well test on the property.
